abstract: |
  Factor construction in empirical asset pricing embeds dozens of methodological choices (breakpoints, weighting schemes, lagging conventions) that existing libraries leave undocumented and unpublished. Researchers who reproduce or extend a factor series have no guarantee their implementation matches the original. We introduce `tidyfinance`, an [R]{.proglang} package on CRAN covering `{r} arrow::read_parquet("data/sorting_variable_information.parquet") |> nrow()` sorting variables across `{r} arrow::read_parquet("data/portfolio_sort_grid.parquet") |> nrow()` specifications. Each construction choice has a documented default and can be varied independently. The package runs from raw WRDS and Compustat data to long-short portfolio returns in a single workflow. A programmatic API and interactive dashboard at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org) provide access to precomputed series. [Python]{.proglang} researchers access the same data and factor library via `py-tidyfinance`. Researchers can reproduce any existing factor series, vary any construction choice, and extend the library to new sorting variables within a single open-source framework.

## Introduction: Constructing financial risk factors {#sec-intro}

Factor returns in empirical asset pricing embed dozens of methodological choices: how breakpoints are set, whether portfolios are equal- or value-weighted, how delistings are handled, and which fiscal-year lag is applied. These choices are consequential, rarely standardized, and almost never published with code. Researchers who reproduce or extend a factor series must reconstruct each pipeline from scratch, with no guarantee their choices match those of the original authors.

No widely adopted, transparent source standardizes factor construction. Current practice relies on informal publication of factor series without code or documented workflows, limiting reproducibility, comparability, and extension.^[Existing resources illustrate the gap: the French Data Library [@fama.2023] provides canonical factors but no code; the Open Source Asset Pricing Project [@chen.2022] focuses on replication; the global factor database [@jensen.2023] targets [Python]{.proglang} only. No unified, open-source alternative exists.]

We introduce `tidyfinance` ([R]{.proglang}, on CRAN): a modular framework for reproducible factor construction. The library covers `{r} sorting_variable_information |> nrow()` sorting variables and `{r} portfolio_sort_grid |> nrow()` total specifications. We document and test every design choice (breakpoints, weighting, rebalancing, sample inclusion) and expose each as a configurable parameter.

The package implements an end-to-end pipeline: data acquisition from WRDS, Compustat, and other common providers; automated variable construction with standard lagging and cleaning routines; and portfolio aggregation with configurable sorting. A programmatic API provides access to precomputed factor series with versioning and batch retrieval. An interactive dashboard at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org) makes the library accessible without code. [Python]{.proglang} researchers access the same data download functions and factor library via `py-tidyfinance`. All software and workflows are publicly available to enable replication, sensitivity analysis, and extension.

@hou.2020 replicate 452 cross-sectional anomalies and find that most fail to survive out-of-sample, attributing failures in part to undocumented construction variation across studies. @chen.2022 respond by publishing code for 212 anomaly portfolios, but their library targets a fixed, documented set rather than a reconfigurable pipeline. @jensen.2023 provide a global factor database without an open construction workflow. `tidyfinance` fills the gap all three leave open: every construction decision is explicit, configurable, and version-controlled, so researchers can trace and vary any assumption systematically.

Among [R]{.proglang} packages for quantitative finance, [tidyquant]{.pkg}, [PerformanceAnalytics]{.pkg}, and [quantmod]{.pkg} support time-series retrieval and portfolio performance analytics. None begins at raw accounting and return data, applies the cleaning and lagging conventions factor construction requires, or exposes construction choices as configurable parameters. `tidyfinance` provides this upstream pipeline in [R]{.proglang} with a consistent API; `py-tidyfinance` extends the same interface to [Python]{.proglang}. Researchers access standardized factor series without rebuilding data workflows in each environment.

## Vignette: A case study in factor construction {#sec-ag}

Our core focus is to present the [R]{.proglang} package `tidyfinance`. We walk through the construction of a single risk factor, asset growth, from raw data to long-short portfolio returns. Each step generalizes to the full library of sorting variables. @fig-workflow-diagram shows the end-to-end pipeline and highlights the `tidyfinance` functions involved at each stage.

You can install the released version of `tidyfinance` [from CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tidyfinance) via:

```{r}
#| label: install-tidyfinance-cran
#| eval: false
install.packages("tidyfinance")
```

You can install the development version of `tidyfinance` from [GitHub](https://github.com/tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance) via:

First install the [pak]{.pkg} package if needed, then install the development version:

```{r}
#| label: install-tidyfinance-dev
#| eval: false
pak::pak("tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance")
```

Once installed, load the `tidyfinance` package.

```{r}
#| label: load-tidyfinance
library("tidyfinance")
```

To illustrate the functionalities of `tidyfinance`, we load a minimal set of additional libraries for data manipulation and visualization.

```{r}
#| label: load-libraries
#| message: false
library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("lubridate")
```

### Data sources {#sec-data-acquisition}

A central design goal of `tidyfinance` is to provide a single, consistent interface, `download_data()`, to a wide range of financial and economic data sources. The vignette only requires two of them (CRSP monthly stock returns and Compustat annual financial statements), but the same function gives access to `{r} nrow(list_supported_types())` dataset types spanning equity returns, fixed-income transactions, macroeconomic predictors, and more. The package serves researchers well beyond asset pricing: macro forecasting (FRED, Goyal-Welch), credit markets (FISD, TRACE), and portfolio benchmarking (index constituents) all use the same unified workflow.

For our asset growth example, we download and preprocess the two required datasets as follows. Before the first WRDS download, users call `set_wrds_credentials()` to store their WRDS username and password securely in `.Renviron`; subsequent `download_data()` calls then establish the database connection automatically.

```{r}
#| label: set-date-range
date_start <- as.Date("1960-01-01")
date_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-crsp-compustat
#| echo: false
crsp_monthly <- arrow::read_parquet("data/crsp_monthly.parquet")
compustat_annual <- arrow::read_parquet("data/compustat_annual.parquet")
```

First, we download data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP). CRSP is a comprehensive database of historical stock market data, including prices, returns, and corporate actions for US equities. It is widely used in academic research for asset pricing, portfolio management, and financial econometrics. 
```{r}
#| label: download-crsp
#| eval: false
crsp_monthly <- download_data(
  domain = "wrds",
  dataset = "crsp_monthly",
  version = "v2",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  add_ccm_links = TRUE
)
```

The CRSP dataset includes monthly stock returns, market capitalization, exchange codes, industry classifications, and excess returns (returns adjusted for the risk-free rate). The `add_ccm_links = TRUE` argument merges CRSP-Compustat linking information, which is essential for merging stock returns with financial statement data in later steps. The entire dataset contains `{r} nrow(crsp_monthly)` stock-month observations for `{r} length(unique(crsp_monthly$permno))` unique stocks, covering the period from `{r} min(crsp_monthly$date)` to `{r} max(crsp_monthly$date)`.

Next, we download data from Compustat, a comprehensive database of financial statements for publicly traded companies. Compustat provides both annual and quarterly data, but for this example, we only use the annual dataset.

```{r}
#| label: download-compustat
#| eval: false
compustat_annual <- download_data(
  domain = "wrds",
  dataset = "compustat_annual",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  additional_columns = c("at", "ib"),
  only_us = TRUE
)
```

Annual Compustat data contains `{r} nrow(compustat_annual)` firm-year observations for `{r} length(unique(compustat_annual$gvkey))` unique firms, covering the period from `{r} min(compustat_annual$date)` to `{r} max(compustat_annual$date)`. The `additional_columns` argument specifies that we want to retrieve total assets (`at`) and income before extraordinary items (`ib`), which are necessary for computing asset growth and applying an earnings filter in later steps. Setting `only_us = TRUE` restricts the dataset to USD-denominated observations, ensuring consistency with the US stock returns from CRSP.

Behind the scenes, `download_data()` performs substantial cleaning and variable construction. For CRSP monthly data (version 2), the function restricts the stock universe to common equity securities of US-incorporated corporate issuers traded on NYSE, AMEX, or NASDAQ. The function computes market capitalization as shares outstanding times price (in millions), sets zero values to missing, and creates a one-month-lagged market capitalization for portfolio weights. Exchange codes map to human-readable labels and four-digit SIC codes map to broad industry groups (e.g., Manufacturing, Finance, Utilities). The function defines excess returns as raw returns minus the Fama-French risk-free rate, and drops rows with missing excess returns or market capitalization. CRSP version 2 already incorporates delisting returns into the return series, eliminating the need for a separate delisting bias adjustment. 

For Compustat annual data, `download_data()` restricts to industrial-format, standardized, consolidated financial statements. The function constructs book equity via stockholders' equity (if this is not available, common equity plus preferred stock, and, as a last resort the total assets minus total liabilities), adjusts for deferred taxes and investment tax credits, and subtracts preferred stock (resolved through a coalesce hierarchy of redemption, liquidating, and par values). Negative or zero book equity values become missing. The function also computes operating profitability and investment ratios from standard Compustat variables, and retains only the most recent observation per firm-year to handle duplicate filings. 

`py-tidyfinance` provides the same `download_data()` interface in [Python]{.proglang}, so researchers can use their preferred computational environment without sacrificing functionality.

@tbl-data-sources provides a complete overview of all data sources accessible via `download_data()` in both `tidyfinance` and `py-tidyfinance`.

| Source | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Ken French's Data Library | Fama-French factor models, portfolio returns, and industry classifications (169+ datasets at daily/weekly/monthly frequencies) | `download_data("famafrench", "Fama/French 5 Factors (2x3) [Daily]")` |
| Global Q | Hou-Xue-Zhang Q5 factor model (market, size, investment, ROE, expected growth) at multiple frequencies | `download_data("globalq", "factors_q5_monthly")` |
| Goyal-Welch Macro Predictors | Macroeconomic predictors: dividend-price ratio, earnings-price ratio, book-to-market, term spread, default yield spread, T-bill rate, inflation | `download_data("macro_predictors", "monthly")` |
| FRED | Any economic time series from the St. Louis Fed (GDP, CPI, unemployment, etc.) | `download_data("fred", series = c("GDP", "CPIAUCNS"))` |
| Yahoo Finance | Daily OHLCV stock price data with adjusted close for any ticker | `download_data("stock_prices", symbols = c("AAPL", "MSFT"))` |
| Index Constituents | Current constituents for 21 major indexes (S&P 500, Russell 2000, DAX, MSCI World, etc.) | `download_data("constituents", index = "DAX")` |
| Open Source Asset Pricing | 213+ monthly asset pricing signals and anomaly variables | `download_data("osap")` |
| WRDS -- CRSP | Monthly and daily stock returns, market cap, exchange, industry, excess returns | `download_data("wrds", "crsp_monthly")` |
| WRDS -- Compustat | Annual and quarterly financial statements with customizable columns | `download_data("wrds", "compustat_annual")` |
| WRDS -- CCM Links | CRSP-Compustat linking table mapping permno to gvkey | `download_data("wrds", "ccm_links")` |
| WRDS -- FISD | Mergent Fixed Income Securities Database with bond characteristics | `download_data("wrds", "fisd")` |
| WRDS -- TRACE | Enhanced TRACE corporate bond transactions with Dick-Nielsen cleaning | `download_data("wrds", "trace_enhanced", cusips = "655844CJ5")` |

: Data sources available via `download_data()` in `tidyfinance` and `py-tidyfinance`. {#tbl-data-sources}

For programmatic discovery, `list_supported_types()` returns all supported datasets as a tibble, making it straightforward to explore available data without leaving the console.

```{r}
#| label: list-supported-types
list_supported_types() |> head()
```

Similarly, `list_supported_indexes()` lists the `{r} nrow(list_supported_indexes())` stock market indexes whose current constituents can be downloaded. Researchers can use these, for instance, to identify the member firms of a benchmark index before constructing portfolios.

```{r}
#| label: list-supported-indexes
list_supported_indexes() |> pull(index) |> head()
```

### Data cleaning and variable construction {#sec-data-cleaning}

We illustrate data cleaning and variable construction using asset growth (AG) as our running example. Asset growth is the year-over-year percentage change in total assets [@cooper.2008], 
$$
AG_t = (AT_t - AT_{t-1}) / AT_{t-1}.
$$

The `add_lagged_columns()` function from `tidyfinance` handles temporal alignment by creating a lagged version of total assets grouped by firm identifier (`gvkey`) with a one-year lag. Non-finite values (arising when lagged total assets are zero or missing) become `NA`.^[For the sake of simplicity we do not show every step of the data cleaning process in the paper. For instance, we apply an earnings filter to exclude firms with negative or zero income before extraordinary items (`ib`), which is a common practice in the literature to mitigate the influence of financial distress on asset growth portfolios. This filter is implemented in the code but not shown in the paper for brevity. We also apply an age filter to exclude firms younger than two years, which is common in the literature to ensure that the sorting variable is based on stable financial information. This filter is also implemented in the code but not shown in the paper for brevity. The factor library API provides preprocessed panels with all these filters applied, so users can access the final sorting variables without having to implement these steps themselves.] 

```{r}
#| label: compute-sorting-variables
sorting_variable_data <- compustat_annual |>
  add_lagged_columns(
    "at",
    lag = years(1),
    by = "gvkey",
  ) |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth = (at - at_lag) / at_lag,
    asset_growth = if_else(is.finite(asset_growth), asset_growth, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(gvkey, date, asset_growth)
```

The next step merges annual sorting variables onto the monthly CRSP stock panel using `join_lagged_values()`. The function aligns fiscal-year-end data with monthly observations through a configurable lag window. Setting `ff_adjustment = TRUE` implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993], aligning fiscal-year data from year $t$ with portfolio formation in July of year $t+1$ through a 12-to-18-month look-back window. The same lagging process generalizes to all sorting variables in the full factor library. The factor library API provides precomputed lagged panels for all variables.

@fig-lagging-illustration contrasts the two lagging mechanisms. The upper panel shows a standard look-back window controlled by `lag` and `max_lag`. The lower panel implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993]: fiscal-year data from year $t$ becomes available only from July of year $t+1$, so all months from July through June share the same lagged value locked in at the previous rebalancing. In both cases, `add_lagged_columns()` selects the most recent observed value within the window.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lagging-illustration
#| fig-cap: "Two lagging mechanisms in `add_lagged_columns()`. Each column represents a data series with observed (filled) and missing (hollow) cells. Dashed rectangles mark the search window; arrows show which value gets matched to each target month."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| echo: false
ts <- 0.94
corner <- unit(4, "pt")

month_labels <- month.abb[c(12, 1:12, 1:7)]
n <- length(month_labels)

x_labels <- 0
x_ff <- 0.8
x_std <- 2.6

obs_pattern <- c(
  TRUE,
  FALSE,
  FALSE,
  FALSE,
  FALSE,
  TRUE,
  FALSE,
  FALSE,
  TRUE,
  FALSE,
  TRUE,
  FALSE,
  FALSE,
  TRUE,
  FALSE,
  TRUE,
  FALSE,
  TRUE,
  TRUE,
  TRUE
)

df_data <- data.frame(
  y = 1:n,
  label = month_labels,
  observed = obs_pattern,
  alpha = sample(seq(0.3, 1, length.out = n))
)

obs <- df_data[df_data$observed, ]
miss <- df_data[!df_data$observed, ]
std_win_left <- 2
std_win_right <- 13
std_matched <- 11

ff_win_left <- 2
ff_win_right <- 13
ff_matched <- 11

target <- 20
tiles <- function(rows, cx, grp_offset = 0, alpha_col = NULL, xsize = ts) {
  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(seq_len(nrow(rows)), function(i) {
      data.frame(
        x = cx + c(-1, 1, 1, -1) * xsize / 2,
        y = rows$y[i] + c(-1, -1, 1, 1) * ts / 2,
        group = grp_offset + i,
        alpha = if (!is.null(alpha_col)) rows[[alpha_col]][i] else NA_real_
      )
    })
  )
}

grp_label <- 0
grp_obs1 <- n
grp_miss1 <- n + nrow(obs)
grp_obs2 <- n + nrow(obs) + nrow(miss)
grp_miss2 <- n + nrow(obs) + nrow(miss) + nrow(obs)

obs1_poly <- tiles(obs, x_std, grp_obs1, "alpha")
miss1_poly <- tiles(miss, x_std, grp_miss1)
obs2_poly <- tiles(obs, x_ff, grp_obs2, "alpha")
miss2_poly <- tiles(miss, x_ff, grp_miss2)

ggplot() +
  # Month timeline: horizontal line with tick marks
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels,
    xend = x_labels,
    y = 0.5,
    yend = n + 0.5,
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  # Tick marks
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.08,
    xend = x_labels + 0.08,
    y = 1:n,
    yend = 1:n,
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Month labels as plain text (centered on ticks)
  geom_text(
    data = df_data,
    aes(x = x_labels - 0.15, y = y, label = label),
    size = 4.5,
    color = "grey40",
    hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Standard column --------------------------------------------------------
  # Standard column: observed
  geom_shape(
    data = obs1_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group, alpha = alpha),
    fill = tf_dark_blue,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  # Standard column: missing
  geom_shape(
    data = miss1_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
    fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = miss,
    aes(x = x_std, y = y),
    label = "NA",
    size = 2.2,
    color = "grey65",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # FF column: observed
  geom_shape(
    data = obs2_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group, alpha = alpha),
    fill = tf_dark_blue,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  # FF column: missing
  geom_shape(
    data = miss2_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
    fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = miss,
    aes(x = x_ff, y = y),
    label = "NA",
    size = 2.2,
    color = "grey65",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # --- Standard: grey arrows --------------------------------------------------
  # Grey arrows: lagging pattern for targets 19-11 (lag=7, max_lag=18)
  # t=19→11, t=18→11, t=17→9, t=16→9, t=15→6,
  # t=14→6, t=13→6, t=12→1, t=11→1
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = x_std + ts / 2,
      xend = x_std + ts / 2,
      y = c(19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11),
      yend = c(11, 11, 9, 9, 6, 6, 6, 1, 1) + 0.15
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.4,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  # Standard window
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = x_std - ts / 2,
    xmax = x_std + ts / 2,
    ymin = std_win_left - ts / 2,
    ymax = std_win_right + ts / 2,
    fill = NA,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std - ts / 2 - 0.08,
    y = c(std_win_left, std_win_right),
    label = c("max_lag", "lag"),
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    size = 2.4,
    fontface = "italic",
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = x_std + ts / 2,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2,
    y = target,
    yend = std_matched + 0.2,
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  # FF grey arrows: Jul Y (pos 8) through Jun Y+1 (pos 19) ALL point
  # to Dec Y-1 (pos 1) — locked in at the previous July rebalancing
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = x_ff + ts / 2,
      xend = x_ff + ts / 2,
      y = 8:19,
      yend = rep(1 + 0.15, 12)
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.4,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  # FF window
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = x_ff - ts / 2,
    xmax = x_ff + ts / 2,
    ymin = ff_win_left - ts / 2,
    ymax = ff_win_right + ts / 2,
    fill = NA,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff - ts / 2 - 0.08,
    y = c(ff_win_left, ff_win_right),
    label = c("max_lag", "lag"),
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    size = 2.4,
    fontface = "italic",
    hjust = 1,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = x_ff + ts / 2,
    xend = x_ff + ts / 2,
    y = target,
    yend = ff_matched + 0.2,
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  # --- Main title at the top of the plot --------------------------------------
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 0.55,
    y = n / 2,
    label = "data |> add_lagged_columns(lag = months(7), max_lag = months(18))",
    color = "black",
    size = 4.0,
    family = "mono",
    hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Panel subtitles --------------------------------------------------------
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std + ts / 2 + 0.35,
    y = n / 2 + 0.5,
    label = "ff_adjustment = FALSE",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 3.0,
    family = "mono",
    hjust = 0.5,
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff + ts / 2 + 0.65,
    y = n / 2 + 0.5,
    label = "ff_adjustment = TRUE",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 3.0,
    family = "mono",
    hjust = 0.5,
  ) +
  # --- Year-change dashed lines -----------------------------------------------
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.95,
    xend = max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 0.75,
    y = 1.5,
    yend = 1.5,
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.95,
    xend = max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 0.75,
    y = 13.5,
    yend = 13.5,
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  # --- Year span brackets -----------------------------------------------------
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_labels - 0.55,
    y = c(1, 2, 14),
    yend = c(1, 13, 20),
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.5,
    xend = x_labels - 0.6,
    y = c(1, 1, 2, 13, 14, 16),
    yend = c(1, 1, 2, 13, 14, 16),
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_labels - 0.75,
    y = c(1, 7.5, 15),
    label = c("Year T-2", "Year T-1", "Year T"),
    color = "grey30",
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(x_labels - 0.95, max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 0.75),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-0.3, n + 0.55),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 10))
```


```{r}
#| label: tbl-ag-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-sectional summary statistics for asset growth (winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles). The table reports the number of firm-year observations (N), the mean, standard deviation (SD), and selected percentiles of the annual asset growth distribution computed from `sorting_variable_data`."
#| echo: false
sorting_variable_data |>
  filter_out(is.na(asset_growth)) |>
  mutate(asset_growth = winsorize(asset_growth, 0.01)) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = mean(asset_growth),
    SD = sd(asset_growth),
    P10 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.10),
    P25 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.25),
    Median = median(asset_growth),
    P75 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.75),
    P90 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.90)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```


Before turning to portfolio construction, we characterize the distribution of asset growth using `sorting_variable_data`, which contains one observation per firm-year and is the natural unit for cross-sectional analysis of annual accounting variables. Because asset growth is an annual characteristic that each firm contributes once per fiscal year, computing summary statistics at this level avoids the artificial replication that arises when the same value is carried forward across multiple months in `sorting_data`.

Asset growth is heavily right-skewed: a small number of firms with dramatic balance sheet expansions (through mergers, acquisitions, or large equity issuances) generate extreme positive values that dominate the mean. We therefore winsorize at the 1st and 99th percentiles before computing location and dispersion statistics. @tbl-ag-summary reports the resulting pooled cross-sectional summary.


@tbl-ag-summary-yearly complements the pooled view by reporting how cross-sectional moments evolve over time. For each calendar year we compute the cross-sectional mean, standard deviation, and median of (winsorized) asset growth, and then summarise those annual statistics across the full sample period.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ag-summary-yearly
#| tbl-cap: "Time-series averages of annual cross-sectional summary statistics for asset growth (winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles). For each calendar year, cross-sectional mean, standard deviation, and median are computed from `sorting_variable_data`; the table reports the time-series mean, minimum, and maximum of those annual statistics."
#| echo: false
sorting_variable_data |>
  filter_out(is.na(asset_growth)) |>
  group_by(year = year(date)) |>
  mutate(
    p01 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.01),
    p99 = quantile(asset_growth, 0.99),
    asset_growth = pmax(pmin(asset_growth, p99), p01)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = mean(asset_growth),
    SD = sd(asset_growth),
    Median = median(asset_growth),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    Years = n(),
    `Avg N` = round(mean(N)),
    `Mean (avg)` = mean(Mean),
    `Mean (min)` = min(Mean),
    `Mean (max)` = max(Mean),
    `SD (avg)` = mean(SD),
    `Median (avg)` = mean(Median),
    `Median (min)` = min(Median),
    `Median (max)` = max(Median)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Having characterised the distribution of the sorting variable, we now turn to `sorting_data`, the firm-month panel that serves as direct input to portfolio construction. @fig-breakpoints shows the 33rd, 50th, and 66th percentiles of asset growth over time. Pronounced spikes during economic expansions and contractions highlight the cyclical nature of corporate investment that portfolio sorts aim to exploit.

```{r}
#| label: lag-sorting-variables
#| cache: true
sorting_data <- crsp_monthly |>
  join_lagged_values(
    sorting_variable_data,
    "gvkey",
    min_lag = months(7),
    max_lag = months(18),
    ff_adjustment = TRUE
  )

sorting_data <- sorting_data |>
  select(date, permno, exchange, ret_excess, mktcap_lag, asset_growth)
```

The resulting dataset merges monthly stock returns with the lagged sorting variable. Each row represents a stock-month observation, containing the information needed for portfolio construction: excess returns, exchange membership, industry classification, lagged market capitalization (for value-weighting), and the sorting variable itself.


```{r}
#| label: fig-breakpoints
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of asset growth over time. Lines show the 33rd, 50th, and 66th percentiles of the cross-sectional distribution of asset growth in `sorting_data`, the firm-month panel used as input for portfolio construction. Asset growth is expressed as a proportion (e.g., 0.2 = 20% annual growth in total assets) and covers the full sample period of the merged CRSP-Compustat dataset."
#| echo: false
plot_data <- sorting_data |>
  drop_na() |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(
    "33%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.33),
    "Median" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.50),
    "66%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.66),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "quantile",
    values_to = "asset_growth"
  )

label_data <- plot_data |>
  group_by(quantile) |>
  slice_min(abs(date - median(date)), n = 1) |>
  mutate(date = date %m+% months(36)) |> # Shift label 3 years to the right for better visibility
  ungroup()

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = asset_growth, color = quantile)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(label = quantile),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Asset growth") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

With the sorting variable constructed and merged onto the monthly stock panel, we now turn to portfolio sorts, the mechanism that translates firm-level characteristics into tradable factor returns.

### Portfolio sorts {#sec-portfolio-sorts}

In portfolio sorts, stocks are ranked each period by their sorting variable and divided into quantile portfolios. Portfolio returns are equal-weighted or value-weighted averages of constituent stock returns. The long-short factor return is the difference between the extreme portfolios, for instance bottom minus top for asset growth, reflecting the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008. Key methodological decisions include the number of portfolios, the exchange universe for computing breakpoints, the weighting scheme, and the rebalancing frequency.

The `tidyfinance` package implements this workflow through three functions. First, `breakpoint_options()` configures the sorting parameters: the number of quantile portfolios and which exchanges determine the breakpoints. Second, `compute_portfolio_returns()` takes the sorting data, applies the specified configuration, and returns portfolio-level returns. Third, `compute_long_short_returns()` constructs the hedge portfolio return from the extreme quantiles.

```{r}
#| label: illustrate-portfolio-helper
cross_section <- sorting_data |>
  filter(date == "2024-12-01") |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth   = rank(asset_growth) / n(),
    mktcap_lag = rank(mktcap_lag)   / n()
  )

n_portfolio <- 2

breakpoints_ag   <- cross_section |>
  compute_breakpoints("asset_growth", breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio))

portfolios_univariate <- cross_section |>
  mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(pick(everything()), "asset_growth",
                                    breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio))
  )

portfolios_independent <- cross_section |>
  mutate(
    ag_portfolio   = assign_portfolio(pick(everything()), "asset_growth",
                                      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)),
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(pick(everything()), "mktcap_lag",
                                      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_dependent <- cross_section |>
  mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(pick(everything()), "asset_growth",
                                    breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio))
  ) |>
  group_by(ag_portfolio) |>
  mutate(
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(pick(everything()), "mktcap_lag",
                                      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Portfolio sort approaches illustrated for a single month (December 2024). Each panel plots stock-month observations assigned to `{r} n_portfolio`×`{r} n_portfolio` portfolios based on asset growth rank (x-axis) and size rank (y-axis), both expressed as percentiles. Colors indicate portfolio cell assignment. The univariate sort (left) assigns portfolios on asset growth alone; the independent bivariate sort (center) assigns each dimension independently; the dependent bivariate sort (right) sorts on size first, then on asset growth within size groups."
common_theme <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, breaks = breakpoints_ag, expand = c(0.01, 0)),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0.01, 0)),
  labs(x = "Asset growth rank", y = "Size rank"),
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
)

p1 <- portfolios_univariate |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = as.factor(ag_portfolio))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(subtitle = "Univariate sort") +
  common_theme

p2 <- portfolios_independent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(subtitle = "Independent bivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p3 <- portfolios_dependent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(subtitle = "Dependent bivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p1 + p2 + p3 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Portfolio sort approaches",
    subtitle = glue::glue("December 2024 — {n_portfolio}×{n_portfolio} portfolios"),
    theme    = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
  )

```

#### Univariate sorts {#sec-univariate-sorts}

TODO: Discuss the subfunctions from within `compute_portfolio_returns()`, such as `tidyfinance::assign_portfolios()`, which assigns each stock-month observation to a quantile portfolio based on the breakpoints, and `?tidyfinance::compute_breakpoints()`, which computes the quantile breakpoints for the sorting variable based on the specified exchange universe. These functions are modular and can be used independently for more customized portfolio constructions, such as overlapping portfolios or alternative weighting schemes.

In a univariate sort, stocks are ranked solely on a single characteristic. We illustrate this with asset growth, forming decile portfolios using NYSE breakpoints and value-weighted returns, rebalanced annually in July.

```{r}
#| label: breakpoint-options-main
options_main <- breakpoint_options(
  n_portfolios = 10,
  breakpoint_exchanges = "NYSE"
)
```

The `breakpoint_options()` call specifies that breakpoints come from NYSE-listed stocks only, a common convention that avoids the influence of small AMEX and NASDAQ firms on portfolio cutoffs. We then pass these options to `compute_portfolio_returns()`.

```{r}
#| label: univariate-sort-ag
portfolio_returns <- compute_portfolio_returns(
  sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = "asset_growth",
  sorting_method = "univariate",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  options_main
)
```

`compute_portfolio_returns()` returns a long tibble with one row per portfolio-month, containing value-weighted (`ret_excess_vw`), equal-weighted (`ret_excess_ew`), and capped value-weighted (`ret_excess_vw_capped`) excess returns. The long-short factor return is obtained via `compute_long_short_returns()`. The `direction = "bottom_minus_top"` argument means the factor is long low-AG stocks and short high-AG stocks, consistent with the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008.

```{r}
#| label: long-short-ag
factor_returns_ag <- portfolio_returns |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

@tbl-univariate-sort-ag summarises the time series of each decile across all three weighting schemes, with the long-short portfolio appended as the final row. A monotone decline from low- to high-AG portfolios is consistent with the negative asset growth premium.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-univariate-sort-ag
#| tbl-cap: "Time-series averages of annualised monthly excess returns for asset growth decile portfolios. Portfolios are formed annually in July using NYSE breakpoints, rebalanced annually. Means are annualised (multiplied by 12). The $t$-statistic tests whether the mean monthly excess return differs from zero. The L/S row is the long-short portfolio (bottom minus top decile)."
#| echo: false
decile_stats <- portfolio_returns |>
  drop_na() |>
  group_by(portfolio) |>
  summarise(
    vw_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
    vw_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n())),
    ew_mean = mean(ret_excess_ew) * 12,
    ew_tstat = mean(ret_excess_ew) / (sd(ret_excess_ew) / sqrt(n())),
    vwc_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) * 12,
    vwc_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) /
      (sd(ret_excess_vw_capped) / sqrt(n())),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(portfolio = as.character(portfolio))

ls_row <- factor_returns_ag |>
  drop_na() |>
  summarise(
    portfolio = "L/S",
    vw_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
    vw_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n())),
    ew_mean = mean(ret_excess_ew) * 12,
    ew_tstat = mean(ret_excess_ew) / (sd(ret_excess_ew) / sqrt(n())),
    vwc_mean = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) * 12,
    vwc_tstat = mean(ret_excess_vw_capped) /
      (sd(ret_excess_vw_capped) / sqrt(n()))
  )

bind_rows(decile_stats, ls_row) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Portfolio",
      "VW Mean",
      "VW t-stat",
      "EW Mean",
      "EW t-stat",
      "VWC Mean",
      "VWC t-stat"
    )
  )
```

#### Bivariate sorts {#sec-bivariate-sorts}

Bivariate (double) sorts control for a second variable, typically firm size (`mktcap_lag`), when forming portfolios. In dependent sorts, stocks are first sorted into groups by the secondary variable; within each group, they are then sorted on the main characteristic. In independent sorts, both sorts apply unconditionally, and portfolios form at the intersections. The factor return averages across the secondary dimension, isolating the effect of the primary variable after controlling for size. @fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper illustrates the three approaches for a single cross-section.

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-sort-ag
options_main <- breakpoint_options(
  n_portfolios = 5,
  breakpoint_exchanges = "NYSE"
)
options_secondary <- breakpoint_options(
  n_portfolios = 2,
  breakpoint_exchanges = "NYSE"
)

portfolio_returns_biv <- compute_portfolio_returns(
  sorting_data,
  c("asset_growth", "mktcap_lag"),
  sorting_method = "bivariate-dependent",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  options_main,
  options_secondary
)

factor_returns_biv <- portfolio_returns_biv |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")

factor_returns_biv |> head()
```

Dependent sorts are appropriate when the secondary variable (here, size) strongly affects the distribution of the primary sorting variable, as is typical for many accounting-based characteristics. Independent sorts treat both dimensions symmetrically and work best when both variables are of equal conceptual interest. The `sorting_method` argument supports both methods (`"bivariate-dependent"` or `"bivariate-independent"`).

## Factor library and API {#sec-library}

### Specification grid {#sec-specification-grid}

The examples above represent single points in a high-dimensional space of methodological choices. @tbl-sorting-decisions summarises the preprocessing decisions that can be varied when constructing factor returns. The full factor library exhaustively evaluates all valid combinations of these choices for each of the sorting variables listed in @tbl-sorting-variables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sorting-decisions
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Preprocessing choices in the portfolio sort grid and corresponding `download_data()` arguments. Italic values indicate the default. For double sorts, the secondary quantiles and exchange choices apply to the size dimension only; for univariate sorts, those rows are not applicable. FF refers to the lag procedure of @fama.1993."

tibble::tribble(
  ~`Preprocessing choice`      , ~Argument                                 , ~Options                                               , ~Description                                                                       ,
  "Size exclusion"             , "\\texttt{exclude\\_size}"                , "None; \\emph{bottom 20\\%}"                           , "Fraction of the smallest stocks (by NYSE market cap) excluded from the universe." ,
  "Exclusion of financials"    , "\\texttt{exclude\\_financials}"          , "\\emph{No}; Yes"                                      , "Drops financial-sector stocks (SIC 6000--6999) from the universe."                ,
  "Exclusion of utilities"     , "\\texttt{exclude\\_utilities}"           , "\\emph{No}; Yes"                                      , "Drops utility-sector stocks (SIC 4900--4999) from the universe."                  ,
  "Exclusion of neg. earnings" , "\\texttt{exclude\\_negative\\_earnings}" , "\\emph{No}; Yes"                                      , "Drops firms with negative earnings before sorting."                               ,
  "Sorting variable lag"       , "\\texttt{sorting\\_variable\\_lag}"      , "3m; \\emph{6m}; FF"                                   , "Lag applied to the sorting variable before portfolio assignment."                 ,
  "Rebalancing"                , "\\texttt{rebalancing}"                   , "\\emph{Monthly}; Annual"                              , "How frequently portfolios are reformed."                                          ,
  "BP: Quantiles (main)"       , "\\texttt{breakpoints\\_main}"            , "3; 5; \\emph{10}"                                     , "Number of quantile groups for the portfolio sort."                                ,
  "Sort method"                , "\\texttt{sorting\\_method}"              , "\\emph{Single}; Double dependent; Double independent" , "Single sort or sequential double sort (by size)."                                 ,
  "BP: Quantiles (secondary)"  , "\\texttt{breakpoints\\_secondary}"       , "\\emph{NA}; 2; 5"                                     , "Groups for the secondary sort variable; only relevant for double sorts."          ,
  "BP: Exchanges"              , "\\texttt{breakpoints\\_exchanges}"       , "\\emph{NYSE}; All"                                    , "Exchange(s) used to compute quantile breakpoints."                                ,
  "Weighting scheme"           , "\\texttt{weighting\\_scheme}"            , "EW; \\emph{VW}; truncated VW"                         , "Return weighting within portfolios."
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    escape = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Preprocessing choice", "Argument", "Options", "Description")
  )
```


We host precomputed factor returns for all specifications on Hugging Face and make them accessible via the `tidyfinance` API. Researchers can retrieve results without re-running the computationally intensive portfolio sort pipeline. An interactive download interface is also available at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org).


The factor library covers `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables spanning seven major categories: investment, profitability, valuation, momentum, intangibles, trading frictions, and financing. The selection follows the cross-section of characteristics studied by @jensen.2023, focusing on variables with established empirical support in the asset pricing literature. @tbl-sorting-variables lists all sorting variables, their long-short direction, and the primary reference for each. For each variable, the full factor library provides precomputed factor returns across all specification paths defined in @tbl-sorting-decisions. We host the complete dataset on Hugging Face at [https://huggingface.co/datasets/tidy-finance/factor-library](https://huggingface.co/datasets/tidy-finance/factor-library). Researchers can also browse and retrieve factor returns through an interactive dashboard at [factors.tidy-finance.org](https://factors.tidy-finance.org).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sorting-variables
#| tbl-cap: "Sorting variables in the factor library. The direction column indicates whether the long-short factor return goes long top-minus-bottom (↑) or bottom-minus-top (↓) of the characteristic distribution."
#| echo: false

tab <- sorting_variable_information |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    direction = dplyr::if_else(
      direction == "top_minus_bottom",
      "$\\uparrow$",
      "$\\downarrow$"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(full_name) |>
  dplyr::select(sorting_variable, full_name, direction, citation) |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "latex",
    escape = FALSE,
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Variable", "Name", "", "Main reference")
  )

tab[1] <- sub("llll", "lp{5cm}ll", tab[1], fixed = TRUE)
tab
```

### The factor library {#sec-library-practice}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 9
#| out-width: 100%
#| dpi: 300
#| fig-pos: p
#| fig-cap: "Sharpe ratios across construction choices. Ridge plots show the distribution of annualized Sharpe ratios of long-short return differentials for each sorting variable across all `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` specifications illustrated in @tbl-sorting-decisions, based on the available sample period per factor. Most variables exhibit substantial variation across specifications, underscoring the sensitivity of factor returns to construction choices."
#| label: fig-sharpe-ratio
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

arrow::open_dataset(
  "data/portfolio_performance.parquet"
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sorting_variable, y = sharpe_ratio)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.3, fatten_point = 0, color = tf_dark_blue) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  guides(col = "none") +
  labs(y = "Sharpe ratio (annualized)", x = NULL) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

@fig-sharpe-ratio shows the distribution of Sharpe ratios across all specifications for each sorting variable. Most factors exhibit substantial variation, confirming that construction choices have material effects on factor performance. To download factor returns from the factor library, simply call
```{r}
#| label: download-factor-library
asset_growth_returns <- download_data(
  "tidyfinance",
  "factor_library",
  sorting_variable = "ag",
  sorting_variable_lag = "6m"
)
```

**Note on `dataset = "factor_library"` defaults:** The defaults reflect one common portfolio construction choice, but may not suit every research question. Always verify that the selected combination matches your intended design.

```{r}
#| label: download-factor-library-fill-all
#| eval: false
download_data(
  "tidyfinance",
  "factor_library",
  sorting_variable = "52w",
  sorting_variable_lag = "6m",
  fill_all = TRUE
)
```

To provide specific requests for handselected ids, users can call

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: download-factor-library-ids

full_grid <- get_available_huggingface_files(
  "tidy-finance",
  "factor-library-grid"
) |>
  dplyr::pull(.data$url) |>
  arrow::read_parquet()

download_factor_library_returns_ids(c(123, 456))
```

## Summary and discussion {#sec-summary}

Factor returns encode their construction history. Two researchers following the same paper can produce different factor series, with no way of knowing why, because breakpoints, weighting, and lagging conventions are rarely published alongside the data. `tidyfinance` makes these decisions visible: the package covers `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables across `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` documented specifications, each reproducible from raw WRDS and Compustat data in a single, version-controlled workflow.

The library currently covers US equities. Construction-choice sensitivity in international markets is beyond its current scope.

The broader implication is methodological. Researchers who disagree about a construction choice can resolve the disagreement empirically: run both variants through the same pipeline, compare factor returns, and report the difference. The API and interactive dashboard extend this accessibility to practitioners who need standardized series without running the full pipeline.

With `{r} nrow(portfolio_sort_grid)` specifications across `{r} nrow(sorting_variable_information)` sorting variables, the library makes systematic sensitivity analysis newly tractable. This opens a path toward meta-analytic evidence on which factor properties are robust and which are artifacts of undocumented defaults.

## Computational details {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: renv-versions
#| echo: false
renv_lock <- jsonlite::fromJSON("renv.lock")
pkg_version <- function(pkg) renv_lock$Packages[[pkg]]$Version
r_version <- renv_lock$R$Version
```

We obtained the results in this paper using [R]{.proglang}~`{r} r_version` with the following packages: [tidyfinance]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("tidyfinance")`, [dplyr]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("dplyr")`, [tidyr]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("tidyr")`, [ggplot2]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("ggplot2")`, [lubridate]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("lubridate")`, [arrow]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("arrow")`, [stringr]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("stringr")`, [forcats]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("forcats")`, [ggdist]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("ggdist")`, and [knitr]{.pkg}~`{r} pkg_version("knitr")`. CRAN hosts [R]{.proglang} and all packages at [https://CRAN.R-project.org/](https://CRAN.R-project.org/). `renv`~`{r} pkg_version("renv")` ensures full reproducibility of the computational environment.

# Internet Appendix {.unnumbered}

## Variable construction {#sec-variable-details}

In this section, we show the construction details for the risk factors. We group them by their underlying mechanism as shown in @tbl-sorting-variables in the Appendix of the main paper.

### Financing

**CDI - Composite Debt Issuance**

Following @lyandres.2008, we compute composite debt issuance as the logarithmic growth rate of book debt (i.e., current debt, DLC, plus long-term debt, DLTT) over the last five years, i.e.,

$$
\text{CDI}_t = \log(\text{DLC}_{t} + \text{DLTT}_{t}) - \log(\text{DLC}_{t-60} + \text{DLTT}_{t-60})
$$

We replace the missing values of DLC and DLTT with zero individually.
Additionally, the sum of DLC and DLTT must be larger than zero, and is set to missing otherwise.

**CSI - Composite Share Issuance**

Following @daniel.2006, we measure composite share issuance from CRSP data as the difference between the change in market equity (ME) (i.e., the shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD) and the cumulative log return (where $r$ is a simple return) in each month from $t$ to $t-60$, i.e.,

$$
\text{CSI}_t = \log(ME_t / ME_{t-60}) - \sum^t_{\tau = t-59}\log(1 + r_{\tau})
$$

**DBE - Change in Common Equity**

Following @richardson.2005, we calculate the change in common equity as the change in common equity (CEQ) over one year scaled by lagged assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
DBE_{t} = \frac{CEQ_{t} - CEQ_{t-12}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

**DCOL - Change in Current Operating Liabilities**

Following @richardson.2005, we measure the change in current operating liabilities as the change in current operating liabilities (i.e., current liabilities, LCT, minus current debt, DLC) over one year scaled by lagged assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
DCOL_{t} = \frac{(LCT_{t} - DLC_{t}) - (LCT_{t-12} - DLC_{t-12})}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

We replace the missing values of DLC with 0.

**DFNL - Change in Financial Liabilities**

Following @richardson.2005, we measure the change in financial liabilities (i.e., the sum of current debt, DLC, plus long-term debt, DLTT, plus preferred stocks, PSTK) over one year scaled by lagged assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
DFNL_{t} = \frac{(DLC_{t} + DLTT_{t} + PSTK_{t}) - (DLC_{t-12} + DLTT_{t-12} + PSTK_{t-12})}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

We replace the missing values of DLC, DLTT and PSTK with 0, if at least one of them is given.

**NDF - Net Debt Financing**

Following @bradshaw.2006, we measure net debt financing as cash proceeds from the issuance of long-term debt (DLTIS) minus cash payments for long-term debt reductions (DLTR) plus net changes in current debt (DLCCH) scaled by the average total assets (AT) over the current and the last year, i.e.,

$$
NDF_{t} = \frac{DLTIS_{t} - DLTR_{t} + DLCCH_{t}}{\frac{1}{2} \big(AT_{t} + AT_{t-12} \big)}
$$

We replace the missing values of DLCCH with zero.

**NEF - Net Equity Financing**

Following @bradshaw.2006, we measure net equity financing as proceeds from the sale of common and preferred stocks (SSTK) minus payments for the repurchase of common and preferred stocks (PRSTKC) minus cash payments for dividends (DV) scaled by the average total assets (AT) over the current and the last year, i.e.,

$$
NEF_{t} = \frac{SSTK_{t} - PRSTKC_{t} - DV_{t}}{\frac{1}{2} \big(AT_{t} + AT_{t-12} \big)}
$$

**NXF - Net External Financing**

Following @bradshaw.2006, we measure net external financing as the sum of net debt financing (NDF) and net equity financing (NEF) as defined above.

### Intangibles

**HR - Hiring Rate**

Following @belo.2014, we measure the hiring rate as the change in the number of employees (EMP) over one year scaled by the average number of employees, i.e.,

$$
HR_{t} = \frac{EMP_{t} - EMP_{t-12}}{\frac{1}{2} \big(EMP_{t} + EMP_{t-12} \big)}
$$

We exclude firms with a hiring rate of zero.

**OL - Operating Leverage**

Following @novy-marx.2011, we measure operating leverage as cost of goods sold (COGS) plus selling, general, and administrative expenses (XSGA), both scaled by current total assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
OL_{t} = \frac{COGS_{t} + XSGA_{t}}{AT_{t}}
$$

**RER - Real-Estate Ratio**

Following @tuzel.2010, we measure the real-estate ratio in two subperiods differently.

(a) Prior to 1983, the real-estate ratio is the sum of buildings (PPENB) and capital leases (PPENLS) scaled by net property, plant, and equipment (PPENT), i.e.,

$$
RER_{t} = \frac{PPENB_{t} + PPENLS_{t}}{PPENT_{t}}
$$

(b) After the end of 1983, the real-estate ratio is the sum of buildings at cost (FATB) and leases at cost (FATL), both divided by gross property, plant, and equipment (PPEGT), i.e.,

$$
RER_{t} = \frac{FATB_{t} + FATL_{t}}{PPEGT_{t}}
$$

Subsequently, we winsorize the real-estate ratios in each fiscal year at the first and 99$\text{th}$ percentile.
The industry-adjusted real-estate ratio is obtained by subtracting the industry average real-estate ratio from each stock-specific real-estate ratio.
We use 2-digit SIC codes to assign stocks to industries.
We always require at least five observations to calculate the industry average each year.

### Investment

**ACI - Abnormal Corporate Investment**

Following @titman.2004, we measure abnormal corporate investments using the variable CE, which is capital expenditures (CAPX) scaled by sales (SALE), then ACI is given by CE scaled by CE from the previous three years minus one, i.e.,

$$
ACI_{t} = \frac{CE_{t}}{\frac{1}{3} \big(CE_{t-12} + CE_{t-24} + CE_{t-36} \big)}-1
$$

We follow @hou.2020 and exclude stocks with sales below 10 million dollars.

**AG - Asset Growth**

Following @cooper.2008, we measure asset growth as the change in total assets (AT) over one year scaled by lagged assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
AG_{t} = \frac{AT_{t} - AT_{t-12}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

**DINV - Inventory Changes**

Following @thomas.2002, we measure the change in inventory as the annual change in inventories (INVT) scaled by average total assets (AT) over the current and the last year, i.e.,

$$
DINV_{t} = \frac{INVT_{t} - INVT_{t-12}}{\frac{1}{2} \big(AT_{t} + AT_{t-12} \big)}
$$

**DNOA - Change in Net Operating Assets**

Following @hirshleifer.2004, we measure net operating assets (defined as $NOA^{int}$) as

$$
NOA^{int}_{t} = (AT_{t} - CHE_{t}) - (AT_{t} - DLC_{t} - DLTT_{t} - MIB_{t} - PSTK_{t} - CEQ_{t})
$$

where AT corresponds to total assets, CHE to cash and short-term investments, DLC to current debt, DLTT to long-term debt, MIB to minority interests, PSTK to the value of preferred stocks, and CEQ to common equity.
Missing values in DLC, DLTT, MIB, and PSTK are set to zero.
Then, the change in net operating assets is the difference between net operating assets of fiscal year $t$ and fiscal year $t-12$ scaled by lagged assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
DNOA_{t} = \frac{NOA^{int}_{t} - NOA^{int}_{t-12}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

**DPIA - Change in Property, Plant, Equipment, and Inventory**

Following @lyandres.2008, we measure the change in property, plant, equipment, and inventory by combining the change in gross property, plant, and equipment (PPEGT) with the annual change in inventory (INVT) and scaling this sum by lagged total assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
DPIA_{t} = \frac{(PPEGT_{t} - PPEGT_{t-12}) + (INVT_{t} - INVT_{t-12})}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

**DWC - Change in Net Non-Cash Working Capital**

Following @richardson.2005, we measure non-cash working capital as

$$
WC_{t} = (ACT_{t} - CHE_{t}) - (LCT_{t} - DLC_{t})
$$

where ACT corresponds to current assets, CHE to cash, LCT to current liabilities, and DLC to short-term debt.
We set missing values of DLC to zero.
Then, the change in net non-cash working capital corresponds to the change in $WC$ from fiscal year $t-12$ to fiscal year $t$ scaled by lagged total assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
DWC_{t} = \frac{WC_{t} - WC_{t-12}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

**IG - Investment Growth**

Following @xing.2008, we measure investment growth as the annual change in capital expenditures (CAPX) scaled by lagged capital expenditures, i.e.,

$$
IG_{t} = \frac{CAPX_{t} - CAPX_{t-12}}{CAPX_{t-12}}
$$

**NOA - Net Operating Assets**

Following @hirshleifer.2004, we measure net operating assets (defined as $NOA^{int}$) as

$$
NOA^{int}_{t} = (AT_{t} - CHE_{t}) - (AT_{t} - DLC_{t} - DLTT_{t} - MIB_{t} - PSTK_{t} - CEQ_{t})
$$

where AT corresponds to total assets, CHE to cash and short-term investments, DLC to current debt, DLTT to long-term debt, MIB to minority interests, PSTK to the value of preferred stocks, and CEQ to common equity.
Missing values in DLC, DLTT, MIB, and PSTK are set to zero.
Then, net operating assets is the net operating assets of fiscal year $t$ scaled by lagged assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
NOA_{t} = \frac{NOA^{int}_{t}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

**OA - Operating Accruals**

Following @sloan.1996 (before 1988) and @hribar.2002 (after 1988), we measure operating accruals until 1988 as

$$
OA_{t} = \frac{(\Delta ACT_{t} - \Delta CHE_{t}) - (\Delta LCT_{t} - \Delta DLC_{t} - \Delta TXP_{t}) -DP_{t}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

where ACT is current assets, CHE cash, LCT current liabilities, DLC short-term debt, TXP taxes payable, and DP depreciation and amortization.
Moreover, we replace the missing values of DLC and TXP with zero.
$\Delta$ represents changes over one year.
From 1988 onwards, we measure operating accruals as

$$
OA_{t} = \frac{NI_{t} - OANCF_{t}}{AT_{t-12}}
$$

where NI is net income and OANCF corresponds to net cash flow from operations.

### Momentum

**MOM - Return Momentum**

Following @fama.1996, we measure return momentum from monthly CRSP returns (where $r$ is a simple return) as the cumulative return from month $t-11$ to month $t-1$ skipping the most recent month, i.e.,

$$
\text{MOM}_t = \text{exp}\left(\sum^{t-1}_{\tau = t-11}\log(1 + r_{\tau})\right) - 1
$$

**RMOM - Residual Momentum**

Following @blitz.2011, we define the 11-month residual momentum (RMOM) in each month and for each stock as cumulative residual returns from month $t-11$ to month $t-1$, scaled by the standard deviation of residual returns over the same time horizon.
Residual returns $\epsilon$ are obtained in each month from regressing monthly simple, excess stock returns from month $t-1$ to month $t-36$ on the Fama and French (1993) three-factor model.
Throughout these rolling regressions, we always require 36 monthly returns.

**RS - Revenue Surprise**

Following @jegadeesh.2006, we measure the change in revenues per share (DRPS) from quarterly Compustat data as quarterly sales (SALEQ) scaled by the product of quarterly shares outstanding (CSHPRQ) times their cumulative adjustment factor (AJEXQ), i.e.,

$$
DRPS_{q}= \frac{SALEQ_{q}}{CSHPRQ_{q} \cdot AJEXQ_{q}} - \frac{SALEQ_{q-4}}{CSHPRQ_{q-4} \cdot AJEXQ_{q-4}}
$$

Then, the revenue surprise corresponds to the change in revenues per share over the last four quarters scaled by the standard deviation of the change in revenues per share over the last eight quarters.
We require at least six quarterly observations for this rolling standard deviation and remove infinite values.
Finally, the earnings announcement date has to be after the fiscal quarter end date.^[We follow the convention of @hou.2020 and do not estimate a random walk model with drift to compute the surprise.]

**SUE - Standardized Unexpected Earnings**

Following @foster.1984, we measure unexpected earnings per share (UES) from quarterly Compustat data as the change in split-adjusted earnings (which are equal to quarterly earnings per share, EPSPXQ, scaled by the correction factor for shares outstanding, AJEXQ) per share from its value four quarters ago

$$
UES_{q} = \frac{EPSPXQ_{q}}{AJEXQ_{q}} - \frac{EPSPXQ_{q-4}}{AJEXQ_{q-4}}
$$

Then, standardized unexpected earnings are defined as unexpected earnings per share divided by the standard deviation of unexpected earnings per share over the previous eight quarters.
We require at least six quarterly observations for this rolling standard deviation.
Finally, the earnings announcement date has to be after the fiscal quarter end date.^[We follow the convention of @hou.2020 and do not estimate a random walk model with drift to compute the surprise.]

**52W - 52-Week High**

Following @george.2004, we measure the 52-week high as month $t$'s closing split-adjusted stock price scaled by the highest daily split-adjusted stock price over the previous twelve months.
We only consider stock-month pairs with more than three valid price observations.

**REV - Long-Term Reversal**

Following @debondt.1985, we measure the long-term reversal effect by the cumulative returns from month $t-60$ to month $t-13$, i.e.,

$$
\text{REV}_t = \text{exp}\left(\sum^{t-13}_{\tau = t-60}\log(1 + r_{\tau})\right) - 1
$$

### Profitability

**CBOP - Cash-Based Operating Profitability**

Following @ball.2016, we measure cash-based operating profitability

\begin{align*}
CBOP_{t} = &\big(REVT_{t} - COGS_{t} - XSGA_{t} + XRD_{t} \\
&-\Delta RECT_{t} - \Delta INVT_{t} - \Delta XPP_{t} + \Delta DRC_{t} \\
&+ \Delta DRLT_{t} + \Delta AP_{t} + \Delta XACC_{t} \big) / AT_{t}
\end{align*}

where REVT is total revenue, COGS are cost of goods sold, XSGA are selling, general, and administrative expenses, and XRD are R&D expenses.
Moreover, $\Delta$ refers to one-year changes, which we measure for accounts receivable (RECT), inventory (INVT), prepaid expenses (XPP), deferred revenues (the sum of current, DRC, and long-term, DRLT), trade accounts payable (AP), and accrued expenses (XACC).
We set the missing values of XRD and all missing changes to zero.

**GPA - Gross Profits to Assets**

Following @novy-marx.2013, we measure gross profits to assets as total revenues (REVT) minus cost of goods sold (COGS) scaled by current total assets (AT), i.e.,

$$
GPA_{t} = \frac{REVT_{t} - COGS_{t}}{AT_{t}}
$$

**O - Ohlson's O-score**

Following @ohlson.1980, we measure O-score with the following linear relation

\begin{align*}
O_{t} = &- 1.32 - 0.407 \cdot \log(AT_{t}) + 6.03 \cdot \frac{DLC_{t} + DLTT_{t}}{AT_{t}} \\
&- 1.43 \cdot \frac{ACT_{t} - LCT_{t}}{AT_{t}} + 0.076 \cdot \frac{LCT_{t}}{AT_{t}} \\
&- 1.72 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{LT_{t} > AT_{t}} - 2.37 \cdot \frac{NI_{t}}{AT_{t}} - 1.83 \cdot \frac{PI_{t} + DP_{t}}{LT_{t}} \\
&+ 0.285 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{NI_{t} < 0 \text{ and } NI_{t-12} < 0} - 0.521 \cdot \frac{NI_{t}-NI_{t-12}}{|NI_{t}| + |NI_{t-12}|}
\end{align*}

where AT corresponds to total assets, DLC to short-term debt, DLTT to long-term debt, ACT to current assets, LCT to current liabilities, LT to total liabilities, PI to pretax income, DP to depreciation and amortization, and NI to net income.
We winsorize all variables except for dummy variables at the first and 99$^\text{th}$ percentile of their respective distribution.

**OPE - Operating Profits to Book Equity**

Following @fama.2015, we measure operating profits to book equity as

$$
OPE_{t} = \frac{REVT_{t} - COGS_{t} - XSGA_{t} - XINT_{t}}{BE_{t}}
$$

where REVT corresponds to total revenues, COGS to cost of goods sold, XSGA to selling, general and administrative expenses, XINT to interest expenses, and BE to book equity.
The definition of book equity is (a) the book equity of shareholders plus (b) deferred taxes and investment tax credit (Compustat item TXDITC or TXDB + ITCB if TXDITC is unavailable) minus (c) the book value of preferred stock.
Regarding (a), the book equity of shareholders is shareholders' equity (SEQ), or the sum of common equity (CEQ) and the par value of preferred stock (PSTK), or, if all previous items are unavailable, total assets (AT) minus total liabilities (LT).
Regarding (b), deferred taxes (TXDITC) or investment tax credits (TXDB plus ITCB) if deferred taxes is unavailable.
Regarding (c), the book value of preferred stock corresponds in the following order either to the redemption value (PSTKRV), or the liquidation value (PSTKL), or if all previous items are unavailable to the par value (PSTK).
We replace missing values of items (b) and (c) with zero.
Moreover, missing values in COGS, XSGA, and XINT are set to zero.

**ROA - Return on Assets**

Following @balakrishnan.2010, we measure return on assets as quarterly income before extraordinary items (IBQ) relative to lagged quarterly total assets (ATQ), i.e.,

$$
ROA_{q} = \frac{IBQ_{q}}{ATQ_{q-1}}
$$

Finally, the earnings announcement date has to be after the fiscal quarter end date.

**ROE - Return on Equity**

Following @hou.2014, we measure return on equity as quarterly income before extraordinary items (IBQ) relative to lagged book equity (BEQ)

$$
ROE_{q} = \frac{IBQ_{q}}{BEQ_{q-1}}
$$

Quarterly book equity (BEQ) is computed as the (a) book equity of shareholders plus (b) balance sheet deferred taxes and investment tax credit minus (c) the book value of preferred stock.
Regarding (a), we measure book equity of shareholders by shareholders' equity (SEQQ), or the sum of common equity (CEQQ) and the par value of preferred stock (PSTKQ), or if all previous items are unavailable by total assets (ATQ) minus total liabilities (LTQ).
Regarding (b), the balance sheet deferred taxes and investment tax credit is TXDITCQ, or TXDBQ, or zero if both are missing.
Regarding (c), the book value of preferred stocks corresponds to PSTKRQ, or PSTKQ, or zero if both are unavailable.
Finally, the earnings announcement date has to be after the fiscal quarter end date.

**TBI - Taxable Income to Book Income**

Following @lev.2004, we measure taxable income to book income as pretax income (PI) scaled by net income (NI)

$$
TBI_{t} = \frac{PI_{t}}{NI_{t}}
$$

We require positive pretax and net income.

### Size

**ME - Size**

Following @fama.1992, we measure size as the natural logarithm of the market equity.
We obtain market equity data from CRSP by multiplying the shares outstanding (shrout \* 1,000, as they are given in thousands) with the corresponding share price (the absolute value of altprc), i.e.,

$$
ME_{t} = \log\left(shrout_{t}*1000*|altprc_{t}|\right)
$$

### Trading frictions

**AMI - Amihud Illiquidity Measure**

Following @amihud.2002, we measure the illiquidity from daily return-to-volume (RV), which is the absolute daily return (r) scaled by the daily dollar trading volume (product of vol and prc), i.e.,

$$
RV_{t} = \frac{|r_{d}|}{prc_{t} * vol_{t}}
$$

Then, the Amihud illiquidity measure corresponds to the average return to volume estimate over the last six months.
We require at least 50 observations for this average and adjust the trading volume of NASDAQ stocks according to @gao.2010.

**BETA - Beta Relative to the Market**

Following @fama.1973, we measure the market beta $\beta_{1}$ from monthly CRSP data.
Specifically, we run the following time series regression over the previous five years

$$
r_{t}^{e} = \alpha + \beta_{1} \cdot (MKT_{t} - R_{t}^{f}) + u_{t}
$$

Moreover, we require at least 24 monthly observations for the regression above.

**DTV - Dollar Trading Volume**

Following @brennan.1998, we measure dollar trading volume from daily CRSP data as the average dollar trading volume (product of vol and prc) from month $t-6$ to month $t-1$ (with at least 50 observations).
Moreover, we adjust dollar trading volume from NASDAQ according to @gao.2010.

**ISKEW - Idiosyncratic Skewness Relative to the Fama and French (1993) three-factor model**

Following @bali.2016, we regress daily excess returns in each month on the three @fama.1993 factor model (with a minimum of 15 daily observations), i.e.,

$$
r_{t}^{e} = \alpha + \beta_{1} \cdot (MKT_{t} - R_{t}^{f}) + \beta_{2} \cdot SMB_{t} + \beta_{3} \cdot HML_{t} + u_{t}
$$

Then, idiosyncratic skewness is measured as the skewness of residuals $u_{t}$.

**IVOL - Idiosyncratic Volatility Relative to the Fama and French (1993) model**

Following @ang.2006, we compute idiosyncratic volatility relative to the @fama.1993 three-factor model as the volatility of residuals from the following regression (with a minimum of 15 daily observations)

$$
r_{t}^{e} = \alpha + \beta_{1} \cdot (MKT_{t} - R_{t}^{f}) + \beta_{2} \cdot SMB_{t} + \beta_{3} \cdot HML_{t} + u_{t}
$$

**MDR - Maximum Daily Return**

Following @bali.2011, we measure the maximum daily (excess) return in each month from daily CRSP data (with at least 15 return observations).

**TUR - Share Turnover**

Following @datar.1998, we measure the daily share turnover of each stock as the number of shares traded (vol) scaled by the number of shares outstanding (shrout), i.e.,

$$
T_{t} = \frac{vol}{shrout}
$$

Then, the share turnover for each firm in each month $t$ is the average daily share turnover over the previous six months (with at least 50 observations).
Moreover, we adjust the trading volume of NASDAQ stocks according to @gao.2010.

### Valuation

**BM - Book Equity to Market Equity**

Following @davis.2000, we measure the book-to-market ratio as book equity (BE) from Compustat divided by market equity (ME) from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
BM_{t} = \frac{BE_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$

The definition of book equity is (a) the book equity of shareholders plus (b) deferred taxes and investment tax credit (Compustat item TXDITC or TXDB + ITCB if TXDITC is unavailable) minus (c) the book value of preferred stock.
Regarding (a), the book equity of shareholders is shareholders' equity (SEQ), or the sum of common equity (CEQ) and the par value of preferred stock (PSTK), or, if all previous items are unavailable, total assets (AT) minus total liabilities (LT).
Regarding (b), deferred taxes (TXDITC) or investment tax credits (TXDB plus ITCB) if deferred taxes is unavailable.
Regarding (c), the book value of preferred stock corresponds in the following order either to the redemption value (PSTKRV), or the liquidation value (PSTKL), or if all previous items are unavailable to the par value (PSTK).
We replace missing values of items (b) and (c) with zero.

**CFM - Cash Flow to Market Equity**

Following @lakonishok.1994, we measure the cash-flow-to-price ratio as income before extraordinary items (IB) plus depreciation (DP) scaled by market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
CFM_{t} = \frac{IB_{t} + DP_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$

We exclude all stocks with negative cash flows.

**DM - Debt to Market Equity**

Following @bhandari.1988, we measure the debt-to-market ratio as short-term debt (DLC) plus long-term debt (DLTT) from Compustat divided by market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
DM_{t} = \frac{DLC_{t} + DLTT_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$

We exclude stocks with missing DLC and DLTT observations.

**EBM - Enterprise Book Equity to Market Equity**

Following @penman.2007, we measure enterprise book equity scaled by market equity as net debt plus book equity scaled by net debt plus market equity

$$
EBM_{t} = \frac{(DLTT_{t} + DLC_{t} + PSTK_{t} + DVPA_{t} - TSTKP_{t}) - CHE_{t} + BE_{t}}{(DLTT_{t} + DLC_{t} + PSTK_{t} + DVPA_{t} - TSTKP_{t}) - CHE_{t} + ME_{t}}
$$

where DLTT corresponds to long-term debt, DLC to current debt, PSTK to the value of preferred stock, DVPA to preferred dividends in arrears, TSTKP to preferred treasury stock, CHE to cash and short-term investments, and ME to the market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD).
Lastly, in this case, book equity BE is computed as common equity (CEQ) plus TSTKP minus DVPA.
Missing observations in DVPA and TSTKP are set to zero.
Additionally, we require that the sum of net debt and book equity, as well as the sum of net debt plus market equity, are positive.

**EM - Earnings to Market Equity**

Following @basu.1983, we measure the earnings-to-price ratio as income before extraordinary items (IB) from Compustat divided by market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
EM_{t} = \frac{IB_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$

We exclude firms with negative earnings.

**NDM - Net Debt to Market Equity**

Following @penman.2007, we measure net debt to price as net debt from Compustat scaled by market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
NDM_{t} = \frac{(DLTT_{t} + DLC_{t} + PSTK_{t} + DVPA_{t} - TSTKP_{t}) - CHE_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$

where DLTT corresponds to long-term debt, DLC to current debt, PSTK to the value of preferred stock, DVPA to preferred dividends in arrears, TSTKP to preferred treasury stock, CHE to cash and short-term investments.
Lastly, missing observations in DVPA and TSTKP are set to zero.

**NPY - Net Payout Yield**

Following @boudoukh.2007, we measure the net payout yield as net payouts from Compustat scaled by market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

\begin{align*}
NPY_{t} = &\big[(DVC_{t} + PRSTKC_{t} + \Delta PSTKRV_{t} \cdot {1}_{\Delta PSTKRV <0}) \\
&- (SSTK_{t} - \Delta PSTKRV_{t} \cdot {1}_{\Delta PSTKRV >0})\big] / ME_{t}
\end{align*}

where DVC are dividends from common stock, PRSTKC is the purchase of common and preferred stock, PSTKRV is the value of the net number of preferred stocks outstanding, and SSTK reflects the sale of common and preferred stocks.
${1}_{\Delta PSTKRV <0}$ is a dummy variable that has value one if the annual change in PSTKRV is negative and zero otherwise.
Moreover, we exclude stocks with negative net payouts.

**OCM - Operating Cash Flow to Market Equity**

Following @desai.2004, we measure the ratio of operating cash flows to price as operating cash flows (OC) from Compustat divided by the market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
OCM_{t} = \frac{OC_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$

Before 1988, we measure OC as funds from operations (FOPT) minus the change in working capital (item WCAP).
Thereafter, we measure OC as net cash flows from operating activities (OANCF).
Moreover, we exclude firms with negative operating cash flows.

**SM - Sales to Market Equity**

Following @barbee.1996, we measure the sales-to-price ratio (SM) as sales (SALE) from Compustat divided by the market equity from CRSP (i.e., the fiscal-year end's shares outstanding, shrout, times the absolute value of their price, altprc, in million USD), i.e.,

$$
SM_{t} = \frac{SALE_{t}}{ME_{t}}
$$
